title: Near any point a smooth map is a matrix, and its determinant is how much area it gains or loses
summary: A map sends every point of the plane to a new point and so deforms the whole plane. Zoomed in, the deformation is a matrix, the Jacobian. Its determinant is the local area scale factor and its sign says whether the plane was flipped, which is exactly the factor needed to change variables in an integral. Chains of maps multiply their Jacobians, and the stretch directions come from the Jacobian's singular values, not always from its eigenvalues.

media.alt: A faint blue square grid from minus 1 to 1 and, over it, the same grid after a map: teal and orange curves that bend like waves and lean toward the upper right, with cells that are stretched in some places and squeezed in others, none folded over.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F2.2 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard multivariable calculus and linear algebra. The figure is the design system's synthetic F2.2 render, so no project number is quoted. Every number and identity in the steps and the worked example was verified symbolically (sympy) or numerically for this page.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the coordinate system stretch, squeeze, shear or fold, and by how much?
read_the_figure.axes: The two axes are the plane the map lives in. The pale grid is the original coordinate lattice; the strong curves are the images of the grid lines under the map.
look_at: Cell size: where the image cells are bigger than the original ones the map expands area (determinant above 1), where smaller it contracts.
Cell shape: squares that become long thin rectangles are being stretched in one direction and squeezed in the other (large condition number).
Whether the curves cross or double back. Crossing grid lines means the map is not one-to-one there: it folds.
Whether the left-to-right and bottom-to-top order of the grid is preserved. A mirrored grid means a negative determinant.
read_the_figure.proves: It shows the geometry of the map directly: every claim about local area, stretching or folding can be read off the cells. It does not give numbers unless a colour map of the determinant is added (class F2.3).
if_wrong: Grid lines that cross each other: the map is singular or not injective there and cannot be inverted.
Cells that collapse to lines: the determinant is zero along that curve.
Different axis scales on x and y: all the cells look stretched and the picture lies about the map.
must_check: Equal axis scales so squares look like squares.
Original grid visibly different from the image grid (colour or weight).
Enough grid lines to see the cells but few enough not to clutter.
A statement of the map's formula or parameters.

terms.meaning: A rule that sends each point of one space to a point of another: here a point of the plane to a new point of the plane.
The matrix of all first partial derivatives of the map. It is the best linear approximation of the map near a point.
The factor by which the map scales small areas near a point; negative if the orientation is reversed.
Which way round a loop of points goes. A reflection reverses it, a rotation does not.
Replacing the map near a point by its value there plus the Jacobian times the displacement.
Computing an integral in new coordinates; the area element picks up the factor |det J|.
Doing one map and then another. Its Jacobian is the product of the two Jacobians, in that order.
A stretch factor of a matrix along one of its principal directions. A circle becomes an ellipse whose semi-axes are the singular values.
A factor by which a matrix scales a special direction without turning it. It is a stretch factor only for symmetric matrices.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value: how unevenly the map stretches.

remember: $F(p+d)=F(p)+J(p)\,d+o(|d|)$: a smooth map is, near a point, a matrix.
$\det J$ is the local area factor. $|\det J|>1$ expands, $<1$ shrinks, $=0$ collapses to a line, $<0$ flips orientation.
Change of variables: $\iint f\,dx\,dy=\iint f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\det J|\,du\,dv$. For polar coordinates $\det J=r$.
Chain rule: $J_{G\circ F}(p)=J_G(F(p))\,J_F(p)$, so determinants multiply. Inverse: $J_{F^{-1}}=J_F^{-1}$.
Eigenvalues of $J$ give stretch factors only if $J$ is symmetric. In general use the singular values; $|\det J|=\sigma_1\sigma_2$.
A grid whose lines cross, or a determinant that changes sign, marks a fold: the map is not one-to-one there.

understand.title: Easy: a rubber sheet with a grid
understand.text: Draw a square grid on a rubber sheet and then push and pull the sheet. Every point has moved to a new place, and the grid lines show how. In any tiny region the rubber is just stretched and turned the same way everywhere, like a straight, uniform pull. Writing that local pull down as a small table of four numbers is the Jacobian. Its determinant is how many times bigger a little square has become.

understand.title: Medium: why the factor appears in integrals
understand.text: To add up a quantity over a region you cut the region into tiny cells. If you describe the region with new coordinates, a cell that is a square du by dv in the new variables is a different size in the old ones: it has been scaled by the determinant. So you must multiply by that factor, or you count the area wrongly. In polar coordinates a cell of width dr and angle step dθ at radius r is nearly a rectangle dr by r dθ, so the factor is r, which is why large circles have more area per unit dr.

understand.title: Hard: composition, inversion and what the determinant tells you
understand.text: Doing two maps in a row stretches and turns twice, so the matrices multiply (the later map's matrix on the left), and the area factors multiply. Undoing a map divides the area factor, so a map with determinant zero somewhere has no inverse there: the plane has been squashed to a line and information is lost. A determinant that changes sign along a curve means the map folds the plane there: the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x^2,y)$ has determinant $2x$, which is negative for $x<0$ and sends both $x$ and $-x$ to the same point.

understand.title: Hardest: eigenvalues are not the stretch
understand.text: It is tempting to read the stretch directions from the eigenvectors. That works only for a symmetric Jacobian. A shear $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ has both eigenvalues equal to 1 yet stretches a circle into an ellipse with semi-axes 1.618 and 0.618, and the map $z\mapsto z^2$ has Jacobian eigenvalues $2\pm2i$ at (1, 1), complex, with no real stretch direction at all, while both singular values are $2\sqrt2$ (a pure turn and uniform scaling). The singular value decomposition $J=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$ is the right tool: rotate, stretch along axes, rotate.

steps.title: A map deforms the plane
steps.note: Each point moves, so the coordinate grid is carried to a deformed grid. The deform workspace draws your own formulas; a wrong formula keeps the last good one. Preset 2 is exactly this.

steps.title: Zoom in and it is a matrix
steps.note: This is the definition of differentiability, with the Jacobian as the derivative. Numerical check with u = x^2 - y^2, v = 2xy at (1, 1) and displacement s times (1, 0.5): the linearisation error was 1.25e-2, 1.25e-4 and 1.25e-6 for s = 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001, a factor 100 for every factor 10 in s, so the error is proportional to s squared.

steps.title: The determinant is the area factor
steps.note: A small coordinate rectangle of sides dx and dy goes to a parallelogram whose sides are the columns of J times dx and dy. The area of a parallelogram is the size of the cross product of its sides. Verified symbolically.

steps.title: The sign and a fold
steps.note: The determinant is negative for x below 0, zero on the line x = 0 and positive above. Points x and -x land in the same place, so the map folds the plane over along the y-axis and cannot be inverted there. A reflection has determinant -1 everywhere but does not fold: it is one-to-one. Atlas S20 example 3 shows a reflection.

steps.title: Polar coordinates and the change of variables
steps.note: The determinant r was obtained symbolically. Check: the integral of exp(-(x^2 + y^2)) over the unit disk is 2 pi times the integral of r exp(-r^2) from 0 to 1, which is pi (1 - 1/e) = 1.98587; a direct Cartesian numerical integral gave 1.98587. Over the whole plane the same calculation gives pi (atlas S14 example 5).

steps.title: Composition and the chain rule
steps.tex: J_{G\circ F}(p)=J_G\big(F(p)\big)\,J_F(p),\qquad \det J_{G\circ F}=\det J_G\cdot\det J_F,\qquad J_{F^{-1}}=J_F^{-1}
steps.note: Verified symbolically for F the polar map and G(x, y) = (x + y^2/4, y): the Jacobian of the composition equals the product exactly, and its determinant is r times 1. The inverse polar map has determinant 1 over the square root of x squared plus y squared, which is 1 over r.

steps.title: Stretch directions: singular values, not always eigenvalues
steps.note: For the shear both eigenvalues are 1 although a circle is stretched into an ellipse with semi-axes 1.618 and 0.618, whose product is the determinant 1. For a symmetric matrix such as [[2, 1], [1, 2]] the eigenvalues 1 and 3 do equal the singular values. The singular values square to the eigenvalues of J transpose J.

steps.title: Where it goes wrong: singular and ill-conditioned maps
steps.note: The shear with k = 1.5 has condition number 4.0. Near a fold the determinant tends to zero and the condition number to infinity: meshes built with such a map have collapsed cells and inverting it amplifies errors. Eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the right-hand side of an ODE are the stiffness ratio of the stiffness page: the same matrix, in a different job.

worked.title: What does the map z squared do near (1, 1)?
worked.problem: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(u,v)=(x^2-y^2,\ 2xy)$ is squaring a complex number. At $(1,1)$ find the Jacobian, the area scale factor, the stretch directions and the image of a tiny square of side 0.01.

solution.text: Determinant (the area factor); in general it is $4(x^2+y^2)$.
Image of a square of side $0.01$.

worked.answer: det J = 8: small areas near (1, 1) are multiplied by 8. The Jacobian is a turn by 45 degrees combined with uniform scaling by 2 sqrt 2, so a circle stays a circle (the map is conformal); the eigenvalues 2 plus or minus 2i are complex, there are no real stretch directions, and the singular values show the true stretch. A numerical check of the mapped square gave an area of 8.08e-4 (1 percent above, the second-order effect of the bending), with 8.008e-6 for a square of side 0.001, converging on 8 times the area.

analyze.q: On the deformed-grid figure some cells look much larger than others although the grid lines never cross. What does that tell you about the determinant, and what would a colour map of it show that the grid does not?
analyze.hint: Cell size is |det J|; colour gives numbers.

analyze.q: The lab's Jacobian presets include x = u + v, y = u - v with |J| = 2 and the polar map with |J| = u. Why is one constant and the other not, and how would the picture of cells differ?
analyze.hint: A linear map has a constant Jacobian; polar cells grow with radius.

analyze.q: A shear and a rotation by 45 degrees both have determinant 1. What is different about how they treat a circle, and which of eigenvalues or singular values reveals it?
analyze.hint: Rotation keeps the circle a circle; the shear does not.

evaluate.q: A mesh generator warps a rectangle with a map and reports no problem because the determinant is positive at every grid point. What could still go wrong between the points, and what would you also compute?
evaluate.hint: A positive determinant at samples does not exclude a sign change between them; also look at the condition number.

evaluate.q: Someone says the eigenvalues of the Jacobian are the stretch factors of the map. Give a counterexample and say when the statement is true.
evaluate.hint: Use the shear, or z squared. Symmetric Jacobian.

create: Invent a map of the plane that is one-to-one but has a determinant that varies from 0.2 to 5. Show its deformed grid and say how you would colour the determinant.
Design a plot that shows at once the determinant (area), the condition number (shape) and the folding of a map, using a single colour scale and contour lines.
Write the change of variables that turns the integral of a function over an ellipse into one over a disk, and give the Jacobian factor.

checks.q: What does it mean geometrically that det J = -1?
checks.hint: Area factor and orientation are two different things.
checks.answer: Areas are preserved (the factor is 1) but the orientation is reversed: the plane is mirrored. A shape drawn counter-clockwise comes out clockwise. A reflection is the standard example.

checks.q: Find det J for the map x = 2u cos v, y = u sin v, and the area of the region u from 0 to 1, v from 0 to 2 pi.
checks.hint: Differentiate with respect to u and v and take the 2 by 2 determinant.
checks.answer: $J=\begin{bmatrix}2\cos v&-2u\sin v\\\sin v&u\cos v\end{bmatrix}$, $\det J=2u\cos^2v+2u\sin^2v=2u$. The area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^1 2u\,du\,dv=2\pi$, the area of the ellipse with semi-axes 2 and 1, as it should be.

checks.q: For the map (x, y) to (x^2, y), why can a map with a non-zero determinant everywhere except one line still fail to be one-to-one?
checks.hint: A non-zero determinant is a local statement.
checks.answer: The determinant $2x$ is non-zero away from $x=0$, so near any such point the map can be inverted. But the points $(x,y)$ and $(-x,y)$ have the same image, so globally two different points collide: the inverse function theorem only gives local inverses. The determinant changes sign across the line, which is the signature of the fold.

checks.q: A Jacobian has eigenvalues 1 and 1 but a condition number of 4. Is it harmless?
checks.hint: Which quantity describes the stretch of a circle?
checks.answer: No. Eigenvalues of 1 only say that two special directions are not scaled. The condition number of 4 means that a circle is stretched into an ellipse four times longer than wide in some other direction, so the map is a strong shear. Use singular values to judge the stretch: it is the shear with k = 1.5 in this page.

checks.q: You have a hand-made warp of an image and need to know whether it folds anywhere. What do you compute and how do you display it?
checks.hint: Sign of the determinant over a fine grid, and a plot.
checks.answer: Evaluate the Jacobian determinant on a fine grid (by differentiation or central differences), and display it as a colour map with a diverging scale centred at zero and the zero contour marked. The zero contour is where the warp folds; any region with negative values is mirrored. Also plot the smaller singular value to see where the warp is close to singular before the fold is reached.
